case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court may excuse (via equitable tolling or other equitable exceptions) the 30-day deadline for filing a notice of removal under 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(1).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(1) (the 30-day time limit to remove a civil action to federal court after receipt/service of the initial pleading); relatedly, removal/remand framework under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1441–1447.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Enbridge argues that the 30-day removal deadline in § 1446(b)(1) is a procedural claims-processing rule rather than a jurisdictional limit, and therefore district courts retain traditional equitable authority (e.g., equitable tolling/forfeiture-based exceptions) to excuse an untimely removal in extraordinary circumstances. Petitioners and their supporting amici emphasize that limitations and filing deadlines are ordinarily presumed to incorporate equitable tolling unless Congress clearly says otherwise, and that this case—involving major interstate/international energy infrastructure and treaty/foreign-affairs implications—presents the kind of exceptional context where equity should permit late removal so a federal forum can address federal issues.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Michigan argues that § 1446(b)(1) sets a firm, mandatory deadline for removal that district courts lack authority to extend on equitable grounds (even if the rule is nonjurisdictional). Respondent and supporting amici maintain that removal is purely statutory; Congress specified a bright-line 30-day rule to promote certainty, prevent disruption of state-court proceedings, and limit federal intrusion into state adjudication. They contend that allowing equitable exceptions would invite case-by-case litigation over timeliness, undermine administrability, and expand removal beyond what Congress authorized; and that, in any event, the facts here do not warrant equitable relief even if such a power existed.
key_precedents: Irwin v. Department of Veterans Affairs (1990)
Menominee Indian Tribe of Wis. v. United States (2016)

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains the Irwin/Holland backdrop that nonjurisdictional deadlines are presumptively tollable, but that presumption is overcome where Congress has adopted a tightly reticulated, bright-line procedural scheme and supplied no textual foothold for judicial extensions. Justice Gorsuch’s emphasis that removal is a purely statutory displacement of state-court adjudication—so courts should not add atextual equitable carve-outs that expand federal intrusion—fits both our separation-of-powers approach and the federalism-sensitive design of §§ 1446–1447. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Hallstrom and Nutraceutical is also significant: even nonjurisdictional time limits can be mandatory, “unalterable” claims-processing rules when the statute’s structure and enumerated exceptions signal strict compliance. A narrow disposition—rejecting equitable tolling of § 1446(b)(1) absent statutory authorization, while leaving waiver/forfeiture and trigger-date questions open—best respects precedent and institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point is the Irwin/Holland presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are equitably tollable, but that general backdrop cannot override the enacted text and the specifically calibrated removal scheme Congress wrote. As Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, removal is purely statutory and displaces state-court adjudication only on the terms Congress supplied; courts therefore lack authority to graft an atextual equitable exception onto § 1446(b)(1)’s command that a notice “shall be filed within 30 days.” Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Nutraceutical reinforces that even nonjurisdictional timing rules may be “unalterable” mandatory claims-processing rules when the statute’s structure and operation—here, bright-line deadlines and enumerated exceptions in §§ 1446–1447—indicate strict compliance. On an originalist/textualist approach, the absence of any textual authorization for tolling, coupled with Congress’s detailed specification of timing rules, forecloses judicially created tolling here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point remains Irwin/Holland’s presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines can be equitably tolled, but that presumption is at its weakest where Congress created a tightly reticulated, administrable scheme to displace state-court proceedings only on specified terms. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, § 1446(b)(1)’s bright-line 30-day command operates alongside carefully calibrated timing rules and limited express exceptions, which is strong textual/structural evidence Congress did not invite additional judge-made extensions. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Kagan’s reliance on Nutraceutical and Hallstrom matters here: those cases confirm that even nonjurisdictional claims-processing rules can be “unalterable” when the statutory design forecloses judicial alteration, and § 1446–§ 1447’s framework does exactly that. I therefore see no legitimate textual hook to graft equitable tolling onto removal, and the practical consequence would be predictable satellite litigation and greater intrusion into state proceedings.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the Irwin/Holland backdrop that nonjurisdictional deadlines are ordinarily subject to equitable tolling, especially to avoid unfairness in extraordinary cases. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief emphasize, § 1446(b)(1) sits within a tightly reticulated removal/remand scheme calibrated for speed, administrability, and respect for state-court proceedings; importing tolling would predictably generate satellite litigation and erode the bright-line certainty plaintiffs and state courts rely on. Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s reliance on Nutraceutical and Hallstrom matters: those cases reinforce that even nonjurisdictional timing rules can be mandatory and effectively “unalterable” when text and structure supply no foothold for judicial extension, and § 1446’s specific timing provisions and enumerated exceptions point against judge-made add-ons. Given removal’s purely statutory character and federalism costs, I still do not see a principled basis to graft equitable tolling onto § 1446(b)(1) absent clearer congressional authorization.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains the Irwin/Holland backdrop presuming equitable tolling for nonjurisdictional deadlines, but here the statutory context matters: § 1446(b)(1)’s “shall be filed within 30 days” sits in a reticulated removal/remand scheme built for speed, administrability, and minimal disruption of state-court proceedings. Chief Justice Roberts’s federalism/administrability concern is persuasive because equitable tolling would predictably spawn satellite litigation over excuses and destabilize the bright-line removal window Congress calibrated in §§ 1446–1447. Justice Barrett’s observation that removal is purely statutory reinforces, on a textualist footing, that courts need a clearer congressional signal before adding an equitable safety valve—especially when § 1446 already contains specific timing rules and exceptions. Nutraceutical (as Justice Thomas emphasizes) confirms that even nonjurisdictional deadlines can be mandatory and effectively “unalterable” when properly invoked, and I do not see textual room to infer tolling authority here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains the Irwin/Holland presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are equitably tollable, but in this statutory context that backdrop gives way to Congress’s chosen text and structure. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, § 1446(b)(1)’s mandatory “shall … within 30 days” sits within a “tightly reticulated” removal/remand scheme whose evident design is swift, administrable channeling out of (and back to) state court—something equitable tolling would destabilize through satellite litigation. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Hallstrom and Nutraceutical is also persuasive: even when a rule is nonjurisdictional, it can still be an “unalterable” claims-processing rule when properly invoked, and nothing in §§ 1446–1447 supplies a textual foothold for judicial extensions. Under a textualist/originalist approach and separation-of-powers principles, courts may not graft equitable carve-outs onto a purely statutory mechanism that displaces state adjudication only on Congress’s terms.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains the Irwin/Holland background presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are tollable in equity, but that presumption is overcome here by Congress’s design choice for a bright-line, administrable removal window that protects state-court proceedings. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on the tightly reticulated §§ 1446–1447 framework and the federalism costs of case-by-case tolling is persuasive, and it aligns with Nutraceutical’s instruction (as Justice Thomas notes) that some claims-processing rules are still “unalterable” when text and structure foreclose judicial extensions. Section 1446(b)(1)’s mandatory “shall … within 30 days” command, coupled with Congress’s inclusion of specific timing rules and limited exceptions elsewhere in § 1446, indicates no room for an extra-textual equitable carveout. Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the Irwin/Holland background presumption favoring equitable tolling for nonjurisdictional deadlines, but § 1446(b)(1)’s command that the notice “shall be filed within 30 days,” read in the context of § 1446’s detailed, enumerated timing rules, indicates Congress chose a bright-line scheme rather than a discretionary equitable overlay. Justice Gorsuch’s emphasis that removal is purely statutory and displaces state proceedings only on Congress’s terms reinforces, under a textualist/originalist approach, that we should not enlarge federal removal authority without a clear textual hook. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s reliance on Nutraceutical usefully underscores that even when a deadline is nonjurisdictional it can still be an “unalterable” mandatory claim-processing rule when the statutory design forecloses judicial extensions, which is the better reading here. I therefore see no basis to recognize equitable tolling absent congressional authorization, while leaving waiver/forfeiture and accrual questions for another day.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the Irwin/Holland presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines are generally subject to equitable tolling, and I take seriously the fairness impulse behind that rule. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 1446(b)(1) sits in a detailed, bright-line removal/remand framework meant to be swift and administrable, and importing tolling would predictably generate satellite litigation and uncertainty for plaintiffs and state courts. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Nutraceutical matters here: even if the deadline is nonjurisdictional, it can still be a mandatory claims-processing rule “unalterable” when properly invoked, and nothing in §§ 1446–1447 supplies the textual foothold we typically require to authorize judicial extensions. Given removal’s uniquely intrusive, purely statutory character (as Justice Gorsuch underscores), I do not think equity can be used to expand federal displacement of state proceedings beyond what Congress specified.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) provides that a notice of removal “shall” be filed within 30 days, and in the removal context—where federal jurisdiction displaces state-court adjudication—Congress’s bright-line timing choice should be enforced as written to protect administrability and federalism. Even assuming the deadline is nonjurisdictional, we have treated many such deadlines as mandatory claims-processing rules that are “unalterable” when properly invoked, absent textual basis for equitable exceptions. Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert holds that a nonjurisdictional but mandatory deadline is not subject to equitable tolling where the statute’s text and structure foreclose it, and § 1446’s design (certainty, swift channeling, and limited intrusion into state proceedings) points the same direction. A narrow holding that district courts lack equitable authority to extend § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day period best respects Congress’s calibration of removal and preserves institutional legitimacy by avoiding a case-by-case equitable regime in an area governed by statute.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) provides a clear textual command that a notice of removal "shall be filed within 30 days" after receipt or service of the initial pleading, and nothing in the removal statutes authorizes courts to extend that deadline on equitable grounds. Because removal is purely a matter of statute, federal courts must adhere to the limits Congress prescribed and may not create extra-textual exceptions that expand federal intrusion into state-court proceedings. This Court has repeatedly held that where Congress sets mandatory deadlines in a statutory scheme demanding administrable, bright-line rules, courts are "not at liberty to create an exception where Congress has declined to do so" (Hallstrom v. Tillamook) and should enforce the rule as written (see also Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert, examining whether the text leaves room for tolling and refusing flexibility where the scheme forecloses it). Even if § 1446(b)(1) is nonjurisdictional, it remains a mandatory claims-processing rule that must be enforced as written when properly invoked, and equity cannot supply authority that the statutory text withholds.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) sets a specific 30-day deadline for invoking the extraordinary, purely statutory remedy of removal, and Congress structured the removal scheme to include particular, express timing rules and exceptions, counseling against judicially creating additional equitable carve-outs. Even when a deadline is nonjurisdictional, we have treated some statutory time limits as “mandatory” and not subject to equitable tolling where the text and structure indicate no exceptions, as in Nutraceutical Corp. v. Lambert (2019). Allowing equitable tolling here would undermine administrability and fairness to state-court plaintiffs—often less-resourced litigants—by inviting satellite litigation and destabilizing reliance on a clear removal/remand framework under §§ 1446–1447. Because Congress did not clearly authorize tolling in § 1446(b)(1) and the statutory design favors a bright-line rule, district courts lack equitable power to excuse untimely removal.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) provides that a notice of removal “shall” be filed within 30 days, and the removal scheme in §§ 1441–1447 is designed to deliver a clear, administrable cutoff that minimizes disruption of ongoing state-court proceedings—workability concerns that weigh strongly against case-by-case equitable extensions. Even if the 30-day limit is nonjurisdictional, this Court has held that some nonjurisdictional deadlines function as mandatory claims-processing rules that are “unalterable” when properly invoked, and the statutory text and structure can rebut any background tolling presumption. Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) provides that a notice of removal “shall” be filed “within 30 days” after service or receipt of the initial pleading, and removal exists only by statute, so federal courts should not add extra-statutory equitable carveouts that expand federal intrusion into state adjudication beyond what Congress authorized. Even if the deadline is nonjurisdictional, it is a mandatory claims-processing rule that, when properly invoked, must be enforced as written; Nutraceutical Corp. v. The Irwin/Holland tolling presumption developed for statutes of limitations governing when a plaintiff may sue the Government does not fit removal’s distinct, tightly cabined statutory scheme in §§ 1441–1447, where Congress chose a bright-line rule to promote certainty and respect federalism. Respecting separation of powers, any exceptions to the removal window should come from Congress, not judicial equitable revision of § 1446(b)(1).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) sets a mandatory 30-day deadline for removal, and even if that deadline is nonjurisdictional, the Court has repeatedly held that nonjurisdictional claims-processing rules may still be "mandatory" when the statute’s text and structure foreclose equitable exceptions. case_analysis.petitioner_position: Enbridge argues that § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day removal deadline is not an inflexible bar and that district courts retain equitable authority to excuse noncompliance in appropriate circumstances. Petitioners and their supporting amici stress that statutory deadlines commonly incorporate traditional equitable doctrines unless Congress clearly precludes them; they contend the Sixth Circuit wrongly treated the 30-day limit as categorically non-extendable. They further contend equitable considerations strongly favor allowing late removal here given the unusually high federal interests asserted in the underlying dispute (including asserted national and international dimensions such as cross-border infrastructure, interstate commerce, and treaty-related concerns).

They also argue that even if equitable exceptions could exist in the abstract, the circumstances here do not satisfy any proper standard for applying them, so the Sixth Circuit’s rejection of late removal should be affirmed.

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest argument remains the usual presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines can be equitably tolled (Holland; Nutraceutical), but here the removal code supplies “good reason to believe Congress did not want” a judge-made tolling overlay. Justice Kagan’s structural point is most persuasive under a minimalist approach: § 1446 already contains tailored timing alternatives and express exceptions (including later-trigger provisions and the bad-faith carveout), which strongly implies courts should not add another atextual exception to § 1446(b)(1). Justice Alito’s administrability concern reinforces the institutional stakes—because § 1447(d) often blocks appellate correction of remand orders, equitable tolling would generate satellite litigation and uncertainty where Congress sought a bright-line, disruption-minimizing rule. Even assuming the deadline is claims-processing (as Henderson-style distinctions suggest), it remains mandatory when timely invoked under § 1447(c), and nothing in the text authorizes equitable extensions in this tightly reticulated scheme.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the general presumption that nonjurisdictional deadlines may be equitably tolled, but that presumption yields to statutory text and structure where Congress has spoken with specificity. Justice Kagan’s structural observation is decisive under a textualist approach: § 1446 sets out multiple explicit timing triggers and exceptions (including later-removal provisions and the bad-faith carveout), so the omission of equitable tolling from § 1446(b)(1) is best read as intentional rather than inadvertent. Nothing in Holland or Nutraceutical authorizes courts to add an extra-statutory exception to a carefully reticulated removal code, and Arellano’s reasoning reinforces that inference when Congress has drafted an exception-laden timing regime. Justice Alito’s administrability concerns are not my primary ground, but they confirm the separation-of-powers problem: recognizing tolling here would be judicial amendment of a rule-like forum-transfer statute.

But as Justice Kagan emphasizes, § 1446 is a tightly reticulated removal code with specific, express timing alternatives and exceptions (including § 1446(b)(3) and § 1446(c)’s bad-faith provision), which strongly indicates Congress did not leave open an unmentioned, judge-made tolling regime for § 1446(b)(1). And Justice Roberts’s administrability point matters here: because § 1447(d) largely blocks appellate review of remand orders, equitable tolling would predictably generate unreviewable satellite litigation and uncertainty that Congress’s bright-line 30-day rule was designed to avoid.

Justice Alito’s administrability concern carries real weight for me in pragmatic terms: because § 1447(d) largely blocks appellate review of remand orders, a tolling regime would generate satellite litigation and instability that in practice burdens state-court plaintiffs (often less resourced) and undermines prompt forum certainty. Even accepting the deadline is a claims-processing rule, the combination of the statute’s “shall … within 30 days” command, Congress’s express exceptions elsewhere, and the federalism-sensitive goal of minimizing disruption to ongoing state proceedings rebuts any default tolling presumption. The general presumption favoring equitable tolling for non-jurisdictional deadlines (Holland v. Florida) is rebuttable, and I would find it rebutted in this tightly reticulated removal framework. Protecting fairness and access to justice for litigants in state court—often including vulnerable parties—also counsels against reopening removal windows through ad hoc equitable litigation that would increase uncertainty and strategic behavior.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) provides that a defendant “shall” file a notice of removal within 30 days of service or receipt of the initial pleading, and that mandatory statutory phrasing—especially in a subsection titled “Requirements”—signals a firm claims-processing rule not subject to freestanding, judge-made equitable extensions absent textual authorization. The structure of § 1446 reinforces that conclusion: Congress created specific, express timing alternatives and exceptions (e.g., § 1446(b)(3)) and elsewhere expressly authorized enlargement when it wanted to (e.g., § 1441(d)), which cuts against implying equitable tolling for § 1446(b)(1). Murphy Bros., Inc. v. Michetti Pipe Stringing, Inc. underscores Congress’s aim of a uniform, bright-line trigger and quick resolution of removal issues at the outset, values undermined by case-by-case equitable tolling that would invite satellite litigation and uncertainty. Because the statute’s text and design supply workable, administrable rules and already contain the exceptions Congress chose, I would affirm that courts may not excuse noncompliance with § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline through equitable tolling or similar equitable exceptions.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) states that the notice of removal "shall be filed within 30 days" after receipt of the initial pleading, and nothing in the text supplies an equitable-tolling or exception clause; in a statute that tightly regulates removal, courts should not add judge-made extensions Congress did not enact. Under separation-of-powers principles reflected in Bowles v. Russell, federal courts lack authority to create equitable exceptions to statutory filing deadlines when Congress has set the time and not authorized tolling, especially in a procedural regime designed to provide clarity and speed and to protect state-court proceedings. The Court’s jurisdictional/claim-processing cases (e.g., Dolan v. United States) recognize a spectrum, but even if § 1446(b)(1) is a mandatory claim-processing rule rather than jurisdictional, it remains a rule courts must enforce when timely invoked—here via § 1447(c). Any equitable-relief argument is properly directed to Congress, not to judicial alteration of § 1446(b)(1)’s plain terms.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline is best understood as a mandatory claim-processing rule that Congress designed to bring clarity and speed to removal and to minimize disruption of state-court proceedings, and the statute contains no textual authorization for judicially created extensions. Even when a time limit is nonjurisdictional, this Court has been reluctant to recognize freewheeling equitable exceptions to congressionally prescribed deadlines, and Bowles v. Russell underscores that courts may not create equitable exceptions where Congress has set a firm time requirement—at a minimum cautioning against expanding equity in timing rules that structure appellate-style review and forum transfer. The removal scheme in §§ 1441–1447 further reflects that Congress specified when and how defects are handled (including procedural defects in § 1447(c)), making it imprudent and unworkable to add an extra-statutory equitable-tolling regime that would invite satellite litigation and undermine predictable administration. Given the statutory structure and practical workability concerns, I would affirm the Sixth Circuit’s refusal to excuse an untimely notice of removal.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) provides that the notice of removal “shall be filed within 30 days” after receipt of the initial pleading, and the removal scheme in §§ 1441–1447 reflects Congress’s choice to prioritize speed, clarity, and prompt return to state court when removal is defective. Although Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007), holds only that courts may not create equitable exceptions to jurisdictional time limits, the textual and structural features of § 1446(b)(1) and § 1447(c) indicate that Congress supplied a mandatory, tightly reticulated procedural framework rather than inviting case-by-case equitable extensions that would undermine predictability in removal practice. In keeping with that framework, any flexibility in removal timing should come from Congress, not judicially created tolling doctrines, because equitable exceptions would generate uncertainty and collateral litigation over timeliness. Accordingly, district courts lack authority to excuse noncompliance with § 1446(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline absent statutory authorization.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1446(b)(1) sets a clear, short, and administrable 30-day period for removal, and the removal framework in §§ 1441–1447 reflects Congress’s design to protect state-court proceedings from disruption and delay; allowing equitable exceptions would invite satellite litigation over timeliness and undermine procedural fairness through unpredictability. Although this Court distinguishes jurisdictional deadlines from mandatory claim-processing rules, even nonjurisdictional time limits can be treated as mandatory when the statutory structure and context demand strict enforcement, and here the removal statute’s emphasis on speed and clarity strongly points against judge-made tolling. Consistent with the restraint principle noted in Pace v. DiGuglielmo, I would affirm on the narrower ground that—whatever the abstract availability of equitable exceptions—this is not an appropriate case to recognize or apply them to override § 1446(b)(1)’s firm deadline. Bowles v. Russell underscores the Court’s insistence that courts may not create equitable exceptions to statutory filing deadlines absent a clear congressional signal, a caution that is particularly salient in the sensitive federalism context of removal.
